stem: \(\square\)PQRS is a parallelogram. PQ = 3.5, PS = 5.3, \(\angle Q = 50^{\circ}\) then find the lengths of remaining sides and measures of remaining angles.
solution:
\(\square\)PQRS is a parallelogram.
\(\therefore \angle Q + \angle P = 180^{\circ}\) ........ interior angles are supplementary.
\(\therefore 50^{\circ} + \angle P = 180^{\circ}\)
\(\therefore \angle P = 180^{\circ} - 50^{\circ} = 130^{\circ}\)
Now, \(\angle P = \angle R\) and \(\angle Q = \angle S\) ........ opposite angles of a parallelogram.
\(\therefore \angle R = 130^{\circ}\) and \(\angle S = 50^{\circ}\)
Similarly, PS = QR and PQ = SR ........ opposite sides of a parallelogram.
\(\therefore\) QR = 5.3 and SR = 3.5

stem: \(\square\)ABCD is a parallelogram. If \(\angle A = (4x + 13)^{\circ}\) and \(\angle D = (5x - 22)^{\circ}\) then find the measures of \(\angle B\) and \(\angle C\).
solution:
Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary.
\(\angle A\) and \(\angle D\) are adjacent angles.
\(\therefore (4x + 13)^{\circ} + (5x - 22)^{\circ} = 180\)
\(\therefore 9x - 9 = 180\)
\(\therefore 9x = 189\)
\(\therefore x = 21\)
\(\therefore \angle A = 4x + 13 = 4 \times 21 + 13 = 84 + 13 = 97^{\circ}\)  \(\therefore \angle C = 97^{\circ}\)
\(\angle D = 5x - 22 = 5 \times 21 - 22 = 105 - 22 = 83^{\circ}\)  \(\therefore \angle B = 83^{\circ}\)

stem: \(\square\)PQRS is parallelogram. M is the midpoint of side PQ and N is the mid point of side RS. Prove that \(\square\)PMNS and \(\square\)MQRN are parallelograms.
solution:
Given : \(\square\)PQRS is a parallelogram. M and N are the midpoints of side PQ and side RS respectively.

To prove : \(\square\)PMNS is a parallelogram.
\(\square\)MQRN is a parallelogram.

Proof : side PQ \(\parallel\) side SR
\(\therefore\) side PM \(\parallel\) side SN ...... (\(\because\) P-M-Q; S-N-R) ......(I)
side PQ \(\cong\) side SR.
\(\therefore\) \(\frac{1}{2}\) side PQ = \(\frac{1}{2}\) side SR
\(\therefore\) side PM \(\cong\) side SN ..... (\(\because\) M and N are midpoints.)......(II)
\(\therefore\) From (I) and (II), \(\square\)PMNQ is a parallelogram,
Similarly, we can prove that \(\square\)MQRN is parallelogram.
_note: BOOK DEFECT — transcribed faithfully, NOT corrected. The 'To prove' names PMNS, but the second-to-last line of the book's own printed proof concludes 'PMNQ is a parallelogram'. PMNQ is not the quadrilateral under discussion: the (I)+(II) argument establishes side PM || side SN and side PM = side SN, which is the one-pair-parallel-and-congruent test applied to P-M-N-S, i.e. it proves PMNS. Verified at 2x zoom on the rendered page — the printed letters are unambiguously P M N Q. Flagged for adjudication.

stem: Points D and E are the midpoints of side AB and side AC of \(\triangle\)ABC respectively. Point F is on ray ED such that ED = DF. Prove that \(\square\)AFBE is a parallelogram. For this example write 'given' and 'to prove' and complete the proof given below.
solution:
Given : In \(\triangle\)ABC, point D is the midpoint of side AB and point E is the midpoint of side AC. Point F is on ray ED such that E-D-F and ED = DF.

To prove : \(\square\)AFBE is a parallelogram.

Proof : seg AB and seg EF are diagonals of \(\square\)AFBE.
seg AD \(\cong\) seg DB ....... (\(\because\) D is the midpoint of seg AB — given)
seg ED \(\cong\) seg DF ....... construction.
\(\therefore\) Diagonals of \(\square\)AFBE bisect each other (each passes through point D, which is the midpoint of both)
\(\therefore\) \(\square\)AFBE is a parallelogram ...by diagonals bisect each other test.
_note: The book prints this worked example as a FILL-IN-THE-BLANK scaffold: its 'Given' and 'To prove' are printed as blank dashes, and its 'Proof' carries five empty boxes — 'seg AB and seg EF are [ ] of AFBE', 'seg AD = seg DB ....[ ]', 'seg [ ] = seg [ ] .......construction', 'Diagonals of AFBE [ ] each other', 'AFBE is a parallelogram ...by [ ] test'. The blanks have been COMPLETED (diagonals / D is the midpoint of seg AB / ED and DF / bisect / diagonals bisect each other) so the row does not ship a holed model answer to students. The book's own step order and reason annotations are preserved; the stem is transcribed verbatim, including its instruction to the student to complete the proof.

stem: Prove that every rhombus is a parallelogram.
solution:
Given : \(\square\)ABCD is a rhombus.

To prove : \(\square\)ABCD is parallelogram.

Proof : seg AB \(\cong\) seg BC \(\cong\) seg CD \(\cong\) seg DA (given)
\(\therefore\) side AB \(\cong\) side CD and side BC \(\cong\) side AD
\(\therefore\) \(\square\)ABCD is a parallelogram..... opposite side test for parallelogram

Measures of angles of \(\square\)ABCD are in the ratio 4 : 5 : 7 : 8. Show that \(\square\)ABCD is a trapezium.
solution:
Let measures of \(\angle\)A, \(\angle\)B, \(\angle\)C and \(\angle\)D are \((4x)^\circ\), \((5x)^\circ\), \((7x)^\circ\), and \((8x)^\circ\) respectively.
Sum of all angles of a quadrialteral is \(360^\circ\).
\(\therefore\) \(4x + 5x + 7x + 8x = 360\)
\(\therefore\) \(24x = 360\)  \(\therefore\) \(x = 15\)
\(\angle\)A \(= 4 \times 15 = 60^\circ\), \(\angle\)B \(= 5 \times 15 = 75^\circ\), \(\angle\)C \(= 7 \times 15 = 105^\circ\), and \(\angle\)D \(= 8 \times 15 = 120^\circ\)
Now , \(\angle\)B \(+\) \(\angle\)C \(= 75^\circ + 105^\circ = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore\) side CD \(\parallel\) side BA...... (I)
But \(\angle\)B \(+\) \(\angle\)A \(= 75^\circ + 60^\circ = 135^\circ \neq 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore\) side BC and side AD are not parallel .........(II)
\(\therefore\) \(\square\)ABCD is a trapezium. ..........[from (I) and (II)]
_note: PRINTED MISPRINT inside the book's own solution, verified at magnification on the render of 0-based p-79 (printed p70): the third line reads "Sum of all angles of a quadrialteral is 360 degrees" — "quadrialteral" for "quadrilateral". Transcribed exactly as printed; no correction applied and no errata bracket written here. Nothing mathematical turns on it: the stated value 360 degrees is correct and the derivation that follows uses it correctly. Checked the rest of this solution for arithmetic defects: NONE — 24x = 360 gives x = 15, and 60 + 75 + 105 + 120 = 360 exactly.

stem: In \(\square\)PQRS, side PS \(\parallel\) side QR and side PQ \(\cong\) side SR, side QR \(>\) side PS then prove that \(\angle\)PQR \(\cong\) \(\angle\)SRQ
solution:
Given : In \(\square\)PQRS, side PS \(\parallel\) side QR, side PQ \(\cong\) side SR and side QR \(>\) side PS.
To prove : \(\angle\)PQR \(\cong\) \(\angle\)SRQ
Construction : Draw the segment parallel to side PQ through the point S which intersects side QR in T.
Proof : In \(\square\)PQRS,
seg PS \(\parallel\) seg QT ........given
seg PQ \(\parallel\) seg ST ........construction
\(\therefore\) \(\square\)PQTS is a parallelogram
\(\therefore\)\(\angle\)PQT \(\cong\) \(\angle\)STR ..... corresponding angles (I)
and seg PQ \(\cong\) seg ST ......opposite sides of parallelogram
But seg PQ \(\cong\) seg SR ......given
\(\therefore\) seg ST \(\cong\) seg SR
\(\therefore\)\(\angle\)STR \(\cong\) \(\angle\)SRT.....isosceles triangle theorem (II)
\(\therefore\)\(\angle\)PQT \(\cong\) \(\angle\)SRT .......[from (I) and (II)]
\(\therefore\) \(\angle\)PQR \(\cong\) \(\angle\)SRQ
Hence, it is proved that base angles of an isosceles trapezium are congruent.
_note: Transcribed exactly as printed from 0-based p-79 (printed p70). Two faithfulness points for the adjudicator, neither corrected here. (1) The book labels the parallelogram "PQTS" in the line after the construction, then names its corresponding angles as PQT and STR; both readings are consistent with Fig. 5.31, where T lies on QR between Q and R. (2) The last step silently identifies \(\angle\)PQT with \(\angle\)PQR and \(\angle\)SRT with \(\angle\)SRQ, which is legitimate because T lies on ray QR and on ray RQ respectively, but the book states no reason for it.

stem: Prove that the quadrilateral formed by joining the midpoints of sides of a quadrilateral in order is a parallelogram.
solution:
Given : \(\square\)ABCD is a quadrilateral. P, Q, R, S are midpoints of the sides AB, BC, CD and AD respectively.
To prove : \(\square\)PQRS is a parallelogram.
Construction : Draw diagonal BD.
Proof : In \(\triangle\)ABD, the midpoint of side AD is S and the midpoint of side AB is P.
\(\therefore\) by midpoint theorem, PS \(\parallel\) DB and \(PS = \frac{1}{2} BD\) ........... (1)
In \(\triangle\)DBC point Q and R are midpoints of side BC and side DC respectively.
\(\therefore\) QR \(\parallel\) BD and \(QR = \frac{1}{2} BD\) ..........by midpoint theorem (2)
\(\therefore\) PS \(\parallel\) QR and PS = QR ................ from (1) and (2)
\(\therefore\) \(\square\)PQRS is a parallelogram.
_note: This worked example spans a page break in the book: its Given / To prove / Construction are printed at the foot of book page 72 (rendered p-81) and the whole Proof completes at the top of book page 73 (rendered p-82), above the Practice set 5.5 banner. Both halves are stitched into this single solution.

context: Choose the correct alternative answer and fill in the blanks.
stem: If all pairs of adjacent sides of a  quadrilateral are congruent then it is called ....
_why: Take quadrilateral ABCD. "All pairs of adjacent sides are congruent" means AB = BC, BC = CD, CD = DA (and DA = AB), so all four sides are congruent. A quadrilateral with all four sides congruent is a rhombus. A rectangle needs only opposite sides congruent, a parallelogram likewise, and a trapezium needs only one pair of parallel sides - none of the three forces all four sides equal.

context: Choose the correct alternative answer and fill in the blanks.
stem: If the diagonal of a square is \(12\sqrt{2}\) cm then the perimeter of square is ......
_why: For a square of side \(a\) the diagonal is \(a\sqrt{2}\). So \(a\sqrt{2} = 12\sqrt{2}\), giving \(a = 12\) cm. Perimeter \(= 4a = 4 \times 12 = 48\) cm. Option A (24) is twice the side, option B (\(24\sqrt{2}\)) is twice the diagonal and option D (\(48\sqrt{2}\)) is four times the diagonal - each is a trap for multiplying the wrong length by 4 or forgetting to divide by \(\sqrt{2}\).

context: Choose the correct alternative answer and fill in the blanks.
stem: If opposite angles of a rhombus are \((2x)^{\circ}\) and \((3x - 40)^{\circ}\) then value of \(x\) is ...
_why: A rhombus is a parallelogram, so its opposite angles are congruent. Hence \(2x = 3x - 40\), giving \(x = 40\). The distractors are the derived angles rather than \(x\) itself: \(2x = 80\) is option B, its supplement \(100\) is option A, and \(4x = 160\) is option C.
_note: BOOK NOTATION SLIP: the four alternatives are printed with degree signs (100 deg, 80 deg, 160 deg, 40 deg), but the stem writes the angles as \((2x)^{\circ}\) and \((3x-40)^{\circ}\), so \(x\) is a pure number and should carry no degree sign. Options transcribed exactly as printed.
